Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 24
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Painter
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 39

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Intrusive Thoughts: Unwanted thoughts, Uncertainty: Uncertainty, Being Watched: Feeling watched or observed
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Dreams: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares, Freeze When Threatened: freeze completely when feeling threatened, Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
  Threat: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
  Memory: Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
  Negative Appraisals: Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am, Inadequacy: I am inadequate, Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere

Vignette:
Two years ago, during a thunderstorm in their shared apartment, the argument escalated until his partner backed him into the hallway. Hands pinned his shoulders against the wall, and the door frame shuddered as it jammed shut behind him. He did not know what would happen next or when the pressure would break. Some fragments remain sharply detailed—the cold sweat on his neck, the exact splinter pattern on the baseboard, the metallic taste of fear—while the minutes before and after dissolve into gray static. He still cannot place whether the shouting came before the shoving or after the door caught. It simply felt as though he was standing in the middle of it all at once. In the weeks that followed, sleep became a calculated negotiation. He began avoiding the early hours, setting alarms to wake him before his mind could slide into the heavy quiet that usually brought dreams. He learned to steer clear of anything that carried his ex’s cologne or echoed his cadence, and he stopped taking certain routes home. When a client at the supply store suddenly raised his voice, his legs locked. He could not remember deciding to do it; he just found himself standing perfectly still until the man moved on. As a painter, his work required him to step into new rooms constantly. Every time he crossed a threshold, his eyes flicked to the doors, the windows, the stairwells. He mapped the escape routes before laying down a drop cloth. When a project ran late, when a client called with a change in schedule, his chest tightened. Delays felt like the ground shifting; he was certain that if things did not proceed exactly as planned, something dangerous would slip through the gap. He would stand by his truck, listening for footsteps on his porch long after the delivery drivers had gone. When he felt the heavy stillness of being observed—sometimes from a neighbor’s window, sometimes from the dark corner of his own living room—unwanted thoughts would surface, looping questions he could not answer. He kept a mental ledger of the job sites, noting which doors opened inward and which windows could be pushed. He could not trust his own recollections; the timeline of those hallway hours refused to line up, and he often caught himself rereading the same line, certain that if he remembered it differently, he might finally understand why it happened. What frightened him most was the quiet certainty that had settled in his bones. He had come to believe that the violence must have been a reflection of his own character, that he had somehow invited it by being inadequate in some fundamental way. His girlfriend, Clara, tried to stay close, but he found himself pulling back. He avoided sleeping in the same bed, afraid that if he relaxed, he would freeze or that she would watch him the way the past had. The distance simply grew, and the inadequacy sat alongside it. He no longer felt he belonged anywhere; the house felt like a temporary holding cell, the studio a room he was just passing through. It was the hesitation that finally pushed him to book an intake. A week ago, while mixing primer, his hand trembled enough to spill the can. He did not just feel startled; he felt certain he had failed, that he was fundamentally broken. He called the clinic not because he wanted to forget, but because he was tired of mapping every room before he could breathe, and he hoped, quietly, that someone might help him figure out how to trust the ground beneath his feet again.
